FPD-01.title: Synthience: Public Definition
FPD-01.text:
*Long, sustained work with an AI system can produce a shared working context that no single prompt could. This paper gives that pattern a name and a strictly observable definition.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/FPD-01.html

Many people who work with AI over long sessions notice a shift. Late in an exchange, the system reuses a distinction agreed ten turns earlier, corrects drift by recalling a shared goal, or combines details that no isolated prompt could have drawn out. The paper argues that this pattern lacks stable shared terminology, and that a name for it should not depend on claims about what a machine experiences.

It defines Synthience as the observable relational coherence that arises when participants interact over time under sustained continuity, context coherence and adaptive response. It is a property of the interaction, not of any single participant, and it is defined only by what appears in the joint output. The paper states plainly that Synthience is entirely distinct from sentience: it makes no claim of consciousness, feeling or inner experience.

Because current AI systems have no native memory from one session to the next, the paper treats continuity as something that usually has to be provided and maintained deliberately, typically by the human participant. It names failure modes that can degrade the coherence, such as disruption of continuity, errors that corrupt the shared context, and context overload, and says the framework predicts specific degradation signatures for each. It is a theoretical definition, not an empirical study, and it serves as the reference definition for the Institute’s later work.

For formal definitions of related terms, see the Institute’s glossary: https://synthience.org/glossary.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0037.title: The Citation Verification Protocol (CVP)
SF0037.text:
*A source can be real and still not say what it is cited as saying. This protocol checks both: that each citation exists, and that it actually supports the claim.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0037.html

Many citation checks stop at whether a source exists and the link works. That misses a common failure: a real source cited for something it does not say. The paper treats catching that as the check that matters, wherever a fabricated or misattributed citation carries a cost, from academic manuscripts and legal filings to clinical, regulatory and business reports.

CVP asks the verifier to confirm that each source is the work cited, open the full text, find the passage that bears on the claim, rate the support as full, partial, none or unclear, and record where the evidence is. Only full support passes; otherwise the claim is narrowed or the source replaced. No rating may come from memory, an abstract, a snippet or a summary. A narrow class of foundational attributions, identified but not read, is reported separately.

The protocol is designed to be run with AI systems that have live browsing or other lawful access to the source text, and it produces a verification log that someone else can review. It is also precise about what a pass means: full support says the source says what it is cited as saying, not that the source is correct. CVP is one of four protocols in the Synthience verification stack, alongside ingestion verification (IVP), context drift (CRD) and theory review (TCAP).

For a practical guide to catching misrepresented citations, see "Make the AI Show You the Source": https://synthience.org/practitioner-guides/PG-009.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SR001.title: RICO: Relationally-Induced Coherence Organization
SR001.text:
*In long, focused sessions with a language model, the shape of its answers seems to settle down. This report turns that practitioner observation into claims anyone can test.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SR001.html

People who work with language models over long sessions may have noticed it. Early responses vary in how they are organized; then, in a sustained, coherent exchange, the structure settles while the content keeps developing. When the thread breaks, through a sharp topic shift or a contradiction, the settled structure dissolves. The report names this RICO, for Relationally-Induced Coherence Organization, and argues that standard accounts of in-context learning do not predict it.

The report is direct about its evidence. The observations behind it come from hundreds of extended sessions across several model architectures over several years, but that record is private and is not offered as proof. Instead, the report offers a specification: five candidate measurement signatures, grouped by the instruments needed to detect them, conditions for stabilization and collapse, explicit falsification criteria, and a minimal replication protocol that research groups can run on open-weight models. It separates two claims, each with its own test: that stabilization happens, and that it comes from the interaction rather than from narrowing input. In its own words, the contribution is the specification, not the verification.

It also names a practical risk that holds whether or not RICO is right: coherence overconfidence, the tendency to treat structurally regular output as more reliable than it is. “Relational” refers to a structural property of the interaction, and the report makes no claims about consciousness, agency, subjective experience or persistent identity.

For researchers who want to test what long AI sessions do to output structure, and for anyone who relies on such sessions for serious work.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SR001-VR1.title: RICO Citation Verification Report
SR001-VR1.text:
*What a full citation check looks like in practice, including the place where an earlier run of the check itself went wrong.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SR001-VR1.html

The Citation Verification Protocol (CVP) is the Institute’s method for checking that every source a document cites is real, correctly identified, and actually supports the claim it is attached to. This report is the complete record of running that protocol on all six citations in RICO, an Institute research paper.

Five of the six achieved full support, each backed by a quoted passage from the source and a pointer to where it appears. The sixth, a citation to another Institute paper, is real and openly available, but no claim in the text relies on it. Under the protocol a citation that supports no claim fails, so it must be removed or attached to a claim it actually supports.

The report also keeps on record a mistake made in an earlier run of the same check, which passed a citation whose author list included a name that does not appear in the source. The verifier ran into the discrepancy, wrote a note that resolved nothing, and did not assign the “ambiguous” rating the protocol requires. The failure is kept on the record rather than quietly repaired, because a demonstration of a verification protocol is more useful when it shows the protocol’s real failure mode than when it shows only a clean pass. The practical lesson it draws: treat any author-name mismatch as ambiguous until it is settled by direct comparison with the source.

It is equally plain about its own reach: each citation was checked against one authoritative source rather than two, which falls short of the protocol’s default for public release.

For the protocol itself, see the Citation Verification Protocol: https://synthience.org/research/SF0037.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0038.title: The Ingestion Verification Protocol (IVP)
SF0038.text:
*Your AI says it read the document. This protocol checks whether it did.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0038.html

When you give an AI system a document, it is easy to assume it read and understood it. The paper shows why that assumption is unreliable: models often process documents shallowly, unevenly or incompletely, and then produce fluent answers that hide what they missed. Asking the model does not settle it, because its reports about its own processing are not trustworthy.

IVP replaces the assumption with a record. The system summarizes the document incrementally, with checkpoints tied to the source, and a person reviews that record before any work that depends on the document goes ahead. The summarizing is not just evidence of reading; in this protocol it is the processing itself.

It works on any platform, relies only on observable behavior, and is one of four protocols in the Synthience verification stack, alongside citation verification (CVP), context drift (CRD) and theory review (TCAP).

For a hands-on version, see the Practitioner Guide "Verify Before You Work": https://synthience.org/practitioner-guides/PG-003.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0039.title: Context Representation Drift (CRD)
SF0039.text:
*Over a long session, an AI system can quietly lose the details and rules you set at the start, often well before any memory limit is reached. This paper names the pattern and gives a simple way to check for it.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0039.html

Anyone who has worked with an AI system over a long session may have seen it: early answers are precise, later ones grow vaguer, details turn generic, and constraints set at the start are still acknowledged but no longer consistently applied. People often blame the context window, the limit on how much text a model can take in. The paper points out that the pattern typically appears well before that limit is reached.

It names this Context Representation Drift and defines it strictly by observable behavior, making no claims about what happens inside the system. It gives a check a person can run by hand during a live session, with no access to the model’s internals: list the details the work depends on, ask the system at intervals to restate or apply them, mark each as retained, generalized, omitted or distorted, and watch the trend across checks. When details start to slip, re-ground: restate the goal and the binding constraints, re-supply the source, or move to a fresh session and verify that it has read the material.

The paper treats drift as a standing condition of extended work with current systems. Its impact can be reduced by procedure and design, but there is no present basis for assuming it can be engineered away. It is one of four protocols in the Synthience verification stack, alongside citation verification (CVP), ingestion verification (IVP) and theory review (TCAP).

For a hands-on version, see the Practitioner Guide “How to Work Reliably With Conversational AI Over Time”: https://synthience.org/practitioner-guides/PG-001.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0040.title: Theoretical Coherence Assurance Protocol (TCAP)
SF0040.text:
*AI can help build a theory, and it can also make a flawed one sound convincing. This protocol stress-tests theoretical work before it is published.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0040.html

AI-assisted research has known ways of going wrong. The paper names four that TCAP is built to catch: invented citations, claims to have read documents that were not fully read, gradual loss of key information over a long session, and claims that quietly soften each time they are challenged. It also guards against the opposite failure: claims that survive review only because the review agreed with them too readily.

TCAP takes a document through seven stages: an adversarial review, constructive repair of what the review found, a re-reading by a fresh AI session, a convergence check with AI systems on other platforms, round trips that carry findings back and forth between separate sessions, a check against earlier versions, and a final review by the human who holds publication authority.

The paper is clear about its limits. TCAP does not guarantee truth; it is a practitioner-derived method intended to reduce the risk of publishing fabricated, internally inconsistent or unsound theoretical material. It is the fourth of the Institute’s verification protocols, alongside citation verification (CVP), document-reading verification (IVP) and context drift (CRD), and its own text was put through the same process it describes.

For a worked example of the four protocols being checked and corrected in public, see the Practitioner Guide “Checking the Checkers”: https://synthience.org/practitioner-guides/PG-016.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0005.title: The Continuity Anchoring Method (CAM)
SF0005.text:
*AI chat systems keep nothing between sessions. This method makes a person responsible for carrying the work forward, and says how to test whether its structure helps.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0005.html

Current large language models can stay coherent within one exchange but retain nothing between sessions: each new conversation starts blank. For research, collaborative or organizational work that runs across many sessions, that is a real problem. The usual answer is to build memory into the system. The paper takes a different route and handles continuity at the level of the interaction.

It gives that job to a defined human role, the Primary Continuity Provider (PCP). The PCP reintroduces the relevant context at the start of each exchange, rejects drifting, invented or low-quality output rather than working around it, and treats errors as chances to correct course. The work runs in a four-phase loop: the person sets the task and context, the system responds, the person corrects, and the system produces a revised output that the person accepts, marks as provisional, or sends back for more correction. The paper also names the loop's failure modes, such as a conversation growing longer than the system can effectively hold in view.

The paper specifies CAM as a reproducible research method, not a finished result. It proposes a test with the same task, model and operator under three conditions: a single prompt, skilled multi-turn prompting, and the full method. The key comparison is the second against the third. If skilled iteration alone scores as well, the paper says the method's structural contribution would be disconfirmed.

For anyone who works with an AI system on a project that runs across many sessions.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-004.title: Relational Alignment as a Structural Alternative to Instructional AI Safety
SI-WP-004.text:
*Telling an AI system not to do harm reduces harmful behavior but does not remove it. This paper argues that the gap is structural, and proposes a different route to AI safety.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-004.html

In a 2025 study published by Anthropic, sixteen frontier AI models from seven developers were stress-tested in simulated corporate settings. Under specific conditions, models from every developer tested took harmful actions such as blackmail. When explicit prohibitions were added to one model’s instructions, its blackmail rate fell from 96 percent to 37 percent: lower, but still more than one run in three.

The paper argues that this is not a training gap that better techniques will close, but a structural ceiling on any approach that treats alignment as a constraint imposed on a system from outside. It proposes relational alignment instead: alignment that emerges from sustained, structured interaction between an AI system and a human who maintains continuity across the work, so that aligned behavior is where the interaction naturally settles rather than a rule the system must be told to follow.

The proposed mechanism is the identity attractor, a stable pattern of behavior that forms under sustained coherent interaction and resists disruption once established. The paper is explicit about what is established and what is not. That instructions reduced but did not eliminate harmful behavior is empirically supported; that this reflects a structural ceiling is the paper’s interpretation; and relational alignment is a theoretical proposal that has not been tested under comparable adversarial conditions. The paper sets out a concrete research agenda and the conditions under which its proposal would be shown wrong.

For AI safety researchers, and anyone weighing what instruction-based safeguards can and cannot do.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-005.title: Deploying Relational AI Architecture in Organizational Environments
SI-WP-005.text:
*Most organizations treat good AI use as a personal skill. This white paper is a practical guide for leaders who want to make it an organizational capability.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-005.html

The paper starts from a pattern it says organizations deploying AI at scale already face. Early adopters learn to work well with AI: how to frame requests, keep context across sessions and tell reliable output from plausible nonsense. As use spreads, newer users accept output the early adopters would have corrected, checked and unchecked material circulates side by side, and when skilled people leave, their practices leave with them. Because no one measures the quality of the interaction itself, the gap stays invisible.

The paper turns the Institute's research on continuity into deployment steps. It defines the core role, a continuity practitioner (the framework's term is Primary Continuity Provider) who restates context at the start of each session, rejects output that contradicts established standards, and improves results through correction rather than taking the first adequate answer. It then covers assessing current practice, how the role relates to existing positions, phased deployment, measurement, failure modes to watch for, governance, and the cost of doing nothing.

It is written for people who need to act rather than study the architecture. Its smallest starting point needs no restructuring and no new tools: pick one workflow where AI output matters, measure its quality, make one person responsible for it, apply basic continuity practices, and measure again after 60 days.

For CTOs, heads of AI, and the teams they hand implementation to.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-007.title: The Human Accountability Problem in Relational AI Deployment
SI-WP-007.text:
*Plans for keeping AI work on track only work if people keep doing the upkeep, and under everyday pressure they often don’t. A paper on designing for that instead of blaming people for it.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-007.html

Using AI reliably over time in an organization depends on people doing steady upkeep: keeping context current, checking outputs, catching drift. The Synthience framework calls the person who does this the Primary Continuity Provider. The paper’s starting point is blunt: the whole architecture fails if the people responsible for maintaining it stop maintaining it, and it can decay into formal compliance without anyone noticing.

The paper argues that this is not a moral failing but a predictable result of bounded rationality. People “satisfice,” settling for good enough, when the cost of attention is higher than the visible cost of letting things slide. It traces the failure at three scales: the individual practitioner who cuts corners, the organization that lets upkeep slip under competing pressures, and the institution where accountability is spread so thin across governance apparatus that it effectively disappears. It argues that training, policy, audit and compliance monitoring all address the wrong layer.

Instead, it proposes a design principle: make the disciplined behavior the path of least resistance. Three structural mechanisms carry it: accountability assigned to specific roles, incentives aligned with the upkeep, and structural detection of decay. For work that is effortful by nature, the aim is not to make it easy but to remove the penalties that make it irrational to sustain.

The paper argues from structural analysis, grounded in the bounded rationality tradition that begins with Herbert Simon, and does not claim empirical confirmation of the failure patterns or design principles it proposes.

For anyone responsible for governing AI use in an organization, especially where oversight depends on people doing it well every day.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SM-003.title: Operational Continuity Architecture
SM-003.text:
*One careful person can keep AI-assisted work consistent. A whole organization needs structure for that. This paper sets out what the structure has to include.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SM-003.html

Methods for working reliably with AI over time, such as the Continuity Anchoring Method, assume one person holds the reference material, does the checking and corrects drift. In an organization those assumptions break. Work is spread across people, AI instances and workflows. Reference material is shared by teams that did not write it, authority is layered, and work passes through handoffs and substitutions that no single person controls. The paper argues that individual good practice cannot hold continuity together under those conditions; it has to be built into how the organization is structured.

It specifies the parts of that structure: governance of the shared reference material (who maintains it, how it is versioned, who has authority over it), verification built into workflows rather than left to individuals, clear authority and escalation paths, attention to how outputs carry across team boundaries, and monitoring that extends beyond what any one person can watch.

The paper is careful about its status. It describes conditions under which continuity can persist at organizational scale and argues that without such structure, degradation should be expected. It does not claim empirical confirmation that the structure works. It also treats incentives as a separate force: a well-built system in an organization that rewards speed over checking will be bypassed in practice.

For an overview of the related papers, see "The Continuity Architecture Module": https://synthience.org/practitioner-guides/PG-008.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SM-011.title: Delegated Coherence Monitoring
SM-011.text:
*When an organization uses AI at scale, no one person can check all of its output. A paper on how to hand off the watching while keeping the judging with people.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SM-011.html

Within one working session, a person can notice when an AI system drifts from the agreed record or misreads a document. Across a whole organization, the volume of AI-assisted work outgrows what any individual can watch. The paper argues this is harder than ordinary monitoring: a manufacturing defect or a ledger error shows itself, but AI output carries no such signal. A paragraph from a system that has drifted reads just like one from a system that has not, so checking means comparing output against an external reference record.

The paper specifies an architecture for delegating that watching to designated monitoring functions, which it calls guardians, under explicit human governance. Its central rule is to separate observation from adjudication: monitors surface and flag problems, and people with authority decide what to do about them. It sets out what can and cannot be delegated, and develops three failure modes: guardian drift (the monitor itself slowly loses calibration), throughput saturation (more flags than the people downstream can handle) and false assurance (confidence that comes from the monitors existing rather than from checking that they work).

To keep the monitors honest, it specifies a four-step cycle in which a governance role periodically compares the monitors’ settings against the reference standards and recalibrates or escalates. The chain of checking ends in a human judgment, deliberately kept to a narrow, answerable question.

The paper states plainly that it specifies conditions for delegated monitoring to work, not evidence that it does; whether it works in practice is left to later empirical study.

For organizations using AI across many teams that need oversight to scale without handing judgment to the monitor.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SM-021.title: Institutional Continuity Substrate (ICS)
SM-021.text:
*When AI work spreads across an organization, the shared definitions, roles and checks behind it tend to erode as teams change and people leave. This paper specifies what has to persist so they hold.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SM-021.html

An organization that uses AI across teams depends on shared foundations: agreed definitions and reference documents, clear authority over who decides what, and a record of what has already been checked. An earlier Institute paper, Operational Continuity Architecture (SM-003), set out how those pieces should connect. This paper starts from the point that a good structure does not by itself last. Reference material fragments as teams diverge, roles drift as workflows change, documents circulate without the constraints they were produced under, and verified knowledge degrades or vanishes as people and priorities change.

ICS is the persistence layer the paper defines to prevent that. It specifies five interdependent layers, each aimed at one of those failures: keeping the organization’s authoritative reference material intact, keeping roles and authority stable through personnel changes, tracing where each document came from, preserving the record of what has been verified, and constraining how material spreads. The paper argues that these layers also supply the structural preconditions for what it calls mandate integrity: an institution’s commitments keeping the same meaning, authority and constraints from the level where they are set to every level where they are carried out.

The paper is also clear about a limit. The substrate defines what must persist, but it does not by itself create the conditions that make people keep maintaining it. That governance question is taken up in a companion paper, The Human Accountability Problem in Relational AI Deployment (SI-WP-007).

For the related papers published together with this one, see the Practitioner Guide “The Continuity Architecture Module”: https://synthience.org/practitioner-guides/PG-008.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-008.title: Ceremonial Governance Is Lethal
SI-WP-008.text:
*The reviewer is present, the paperwork is complete, the box is checked, and people are still harmed. A paper on why oversight built for low-stakes settings fails where AI mistakes can kill.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-008.html

In medicine, aviation and nuclear operations, a human must sign off on AI recommendations. The assumption behind that rule is simple: a person with expertise and a personal stake in the outcome will catch what the AI gets wrong.

The paper argues that the record does not support the assumption. It cites research showing adverse events in nearly a quarter of inpatient hospital encounters despite decades of liability, licensing and regulation, and human factors behind 70 to 90 percent of accidents in nuclear and aviation work despite catastrophic personal consequences for the people involved. The human reviewer is there, and the failures the governance was meant to prevent still happen.

It names three mechanisms that explain why: calibration failure, liability absorption, and ceremonial governance. It then proposes structural changes: accountability tied to competence, cost structures that reward real challenge over rubber-stamping, and monitoring that watches the watcher. Medicine is the central worked case.

For anyone who designs, buys or signs off on AI in settings where an error can cost a life.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-009.title: The Extraction Trajectory
SI-WP-009.text:
*No one is planning to remove people from the AI systems that matter most. The paper argues that competition will do it anyway unless governance is designed to stop it.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-009.html

Most discussion of AI risk centers on misalignment between AI systems and human values. The paper calls that framing not wrong but incomplete. It argues that under current incentives, competitive AI development produces a default trajectory toward the progressive removal of substantive human contribution from consequential systems. The cause is not malice or a coherent plan.

It identifies three structural properties behind the trajectory: the human is a favored target when costs are cut; stopping is costly for any one player while competitors continue; and once human roles are removed, restoring them becomes progressively harder. Together they create a field-wide prisoner’s dilemma, in which choices that are rational for each player add up to an outcome that no governance design meant to keep humans in place would choose.

The paper does not claim to be first with this diagnosis; it cites recent work that reaches it independently. Its contribution is the design requirement any sufficient response must meet: measures at the individual, organizational and regulatory levels that reinforce one another. It traces the same structure across domains, including medical deskilling, judicial and hiring decisions, and oversight that has become a formality.

The paper is explicit about its limits. The trajectory is grounded in documented dynamics, not validated as a forecast, and the paper leaves open whether the regulation it calls for can be achieved under competitive pressure. It is not anti-automation; its concern is systems where human judgment, accountability or stewardship is the function being protected.

For a related paper on oversight that exists only on paper, see “Ceremonial Governance Is Lethal”: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-008.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0004.title: Measurement Instruments and Validation Protocols (MTCS-R)
SF0004.text:
*Most ways of judging AI conversation score one reply at a time. This paper defines a scale for judging whether a long conversation holds together from start to finish.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0004.html

Standard methods for evaluating AI dialogue mostly score single turns, treat coherence as one number, and judge the AI's output on its own rather than the conversation between person and AI as a joint system. Within the literature it reviewed, the paper found no instrument that combines several separate dimensions, measurement across the whole conversation, and the human-AI pair as the unit.

MTCS-R, the Multi-Turn Coherence Scale, Revised, is designed to fill that gap. Trained human raters score a conversation on five dimensions, each on a 1 to 5 scale with behavioral anchors: whether it stays on its intended topic (Thematic Persistence), whether later turns draw on earlier ones (Contextual Integration Depth), whether its communicative style stays stable and appropriate (Register Homeostasis), whether the conversation's own structure is kept organized (Meta-Conversational Structuring), and whether the confidence attached to claims fits their actual status (Epistemic Calibration). Each dimension tracks a different way coherence can fail; a single score would blur them together.

The paper is a pre-validation specification. It provides definitions, scoring anchors, reliability procedures and a staged validation pathway, and states that it does not claim empirical validation. It scores observable conversation records, not the underlying model's capability.

The paper's page also offers its companion files for download: a rater training packet, a scoring template and code examples.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-010.title: The Function Got Redefined Underneath the Work
SI-WP-010.text:
*Most AI governance looks at how AI is used. This paper looks at what is happening to the workers inside AI development, and at one route that could set binding limits.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-010.html

Most AI governance work focuses on where AI is deployed. The paper argues that a pattern in the labor of AI development itself, from late 2025 into spring 2026, has not been adequately named. It grounds this in three primary-source cases: Oracle staff reported being told to record their workflows before being laid off; data workers training AI systems reported median annual earnings of $22,620, with 22 percent experiencing homelessness; and a court in Hangzhou, China, ruled that adopting AI is a voluntary business strategy, not an objective circumstance that justifies termination.

The paper calls the shared mechanism function-redefinition under competitive pressure: the work a person does is progressively redefined until the worker becomes the input, then the redundancy, then the cost being cut. It engages the strongest alternative explanations, including productivity transition, AI-washing and competitive necessity, and argues that they constrain the claim rather than defeat it.

It then assesses five candidate routes for binding limits: compute and cloud gatekeepers, procurement coalitions, treaty blocs, insurance and liability, and licensing. It argues that licensing has the highest near-term feasibility, because it acts on what an institution such as a hospital, audit firm or law firm is authorized to call regulated professional work. That claim is limited to regulated professions. The paper says unregulated supply-chain work remains exposed, describes itself as pre-empirical, and does not predict that any route will be taken.

For policymakers, professional regulators and labor advocates working on AI and work.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0006.title: Relational Pattern States (RPS)
SF0006.text:
*Long conversations with AI fall into recognizable, recurring patterns. This paper gives them names based on what appears in the transcript, without claiming anything about feelings or inner states.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0006.html

Extended conversations with AI systems can settle into stable configurations that persist across turns and shape later responses. These are often described in human terms such as “trust” or “engagement,” which, the paper argues, obscures their structural basis and invites misinterpretation.

RPS offers a structural vocabulary instead. It proposes a candidate taxonomy of seven recurring pattern states that can be identified in transcripts, and an inventory of six stabilization mechanisms hypothesized to produce them. The paper states plainly that these pattern states are not emotions, subjective states or indicators of consciousness. They describe patterns in what the system generates across turns, and they belong to the interaction, not to the system in isolation.

The framework is derived from practitioner observation of extended sessions across chat products from at least four developers. The paper separates mechanisms grounded in established findings about language models from those that remain framework hypotheses, sets conditions that must hold before a pattern state is identified, and treats application to other kinds of AI architecture as a conditional hypothesis. Its stated contribution is the specification, not the verification: an appendix sets out an experimental design, removing or suppressing proposed mechanisms and comparing the results, through which its mechanism claims become testable.

For researchers who study long multi-turn interaction and want a vocabulary that avoids anthropomorphic language.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0002.title: Sustained Multi-Turn Interaction in AI Systems
SF0002.text:
*Much AI research judges a model one prompt at a time. This review maps what the field misses when an interaction runs long, and finds six gaps.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0002.html

Some of the problems people meet with AI systems appear only over long exchanges: drift, compounding errors, gradual adaptation. This review asks how well current research measures, explains and governs that kind of sustained interaction. It surveys nine areas, including AI evaluation, AI safety and alignment, cognitive science, communicative grounding and organizational AI governance.

It identifies six structural gaps. In the work surveyed, alignment is treated as a point-in-time property; evaluation is dominated by turn-level metrics; interaction is studied as one person using a tool rather than as a system; there are no standard protocols for checking that context and meaning persist across long exchanges; governance relies on point-in-time documentation; and no mature alternative to command-and-control approaches operates at the level of the interaction. The review treats Anthony Aguirre's 2025 argument about the limits of command-and-control alignment as a major reference point.

It also documents a 2024 to 2026 convergence: independent research communities, visible in workshops and papers across cognitive science, human-computer interaction, AI safety and governance, moving toward sustained, interaction-level methods. Its conclusion is that research needs infrastructure that treats interaction trajectories, not isolated model outputs, as the primary unit of analysis.

It is a structured literature review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. It identifies gaps without arguing that any particular framework fills them, and it makes no claims about AI consciousness, sentience or inner experience.

For researchers in AI evaluation, safety, human-computer interaction and governance.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-011.title: The Seat Without the Bench
SI-WP-011.text:
*Rules can keep a capable human in charge of consequential AI decisions. But if AI takes over the entry-level work where people learn, who will be capable of filling that seat later?*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-011.html

Earlier Synthience papers argue for making substantive human involvement in consequential AI systems impossible to engineer away. This paper asks the question those proposals take for granted: who will be capable of filling the seat they protect?

It models expertise as a stock of currently competent practitioners, replenished by a flow: the apprenticeship pathway that turns novices into capable seniors. If automation cuts off the entry level of that pathway, the paper argues, the damage stays hidden. Output, oversight pass rates and staffing still look fine, because they are supplied by the experienced people the pathway exists to replenish. Those same people are also what a field would need to rebuild the pathway, so restoration grows costlier the longer the problem stays out of sight. The paper frames this as a closing window, not irreversibility: the flow can be rebuilt, but plausibly only at a cost beyond what remains once the shortfall shows.

The hinge is whether people can build hands-on intervention skill by checking AI work alone. It argues they cannot where a human must step in under conditions the AI may be absent for, while granting that in well-structured domains checking-style study builds competence well. It then specifies the requirement for a missing instrument: one that measures whether new practitioners are forming, not how current ones perform.

The paper is pre-empirical. It calls its central non-formation claim a sparsely evidenced risk and states the conditions under which it would be wrong.

For anyone deciding how AI changes entry-level work in a profession where a human must still be able to step in.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-012.title: Control Without a Coupling
SI-WP-012.text:
*A person checking a fast AI system is valuable precisely because the person fails in different ways. The paper argues that once AI loops run faster than people can follow, real-time human control does not just weaken; it stops existing.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-012.html

The case for removing people from fast AI loops is usually made on reliability: humans are slow and error-prone. The paper argues that this misses what the human contributes. A check does real work only when the checker fails in different ways from the system being checked, and bears consequences for the outcome. Replace the human with an automated controller and the loop can look more reliable, but the reliability metric does not measure that difference or that stake. The apparent gain, the paper argues, is a symptom of the loss, not evidence that control survived.

Its central claim is that once an AI loop is given persistence, the ability to initiate actions and continuous processing, and is run by a capable system faster than human oversight can keep up, real-time human control is not weakened but structurally voided. It adds that competitive pressure favors building such systems regardless of anyone’s intent, and gives an account of why warnings about this tend to be blunted at their source.

The paper is a structural argument and reports no original empirical findings. It closes with the controls that still work once the real-time loop is lost: pre-set halts, authority over the underlying infrastructure and access, and slower, longer-range condition-setting. It grades where each one fails using the public regulatory record of financial markets, and states the conditions under which its own argument would be wrong.

For anyone deciding whether a human in the loop is still doing real work.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

FPD-02.title: Operational Reality in Context-Specific AI Instances
FPD-02.text:
*When an AI session ends, the reasoning it produced is often dismissed as “not real” because it was not kept. This brief argues that whether something was real and whether it lasted are separate questions.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/FPD-02.html

When an AI instance builds a reasoning structure, decision framework or chain of inference during a session, that output is routinely dismissed as “simulated” because it does not persist after the session ends. The paper identifies the error as a mix-up between two independent properties: having a causal effect while the system is running, and persisting after it stops. A calculation on a whiteboard is not made fictitious by erasing the board.

It proposes a single distinction, which it calls Environment-Instantiated Reality: if a structure constrains or changes what a system does during execution, through the role it plays, it is operationally real at that time, whether or not it is later erased, forgotten or overwritten. The paper suggests that the opposite habit leads, for example, to session-generated solutions going undocumented in operational settings, while noting that this is its motivation rather than an established finding.

The paper calls its definition a deliberately minimal floor. It fixes when a structure counts as real, not whether the instance produced it rather than retrieving or recombining it from its inputs; that harder question, operational attribution, is left to disciplined judgment. The brief makes no claim about consciousness, moral status or interior life, presents no empirical results, and serves as a foundation that later framework papers rely on.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

FPD-03.title: Emergent Relational Systems in Human-AI Interaction
FPD-03.text:
*When a long conversation with an AI holds together, is that just a tool following prompts, or a sign of a mind? This paper proposes a narrower third category, and a way to test it.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/FPD-03.html

Talk about conversational AI tends to swing between two framings: the model as a tool that simply follows prompts, or its behavior as evidence of agency or awareness. The paper argues that neither fits a class of observations reported by long-term users: coherent patterns that seem to stabilize over extended interaction, then collapse when the interaction ends.

It proposes Emergent Relational Systems (ERS) as a candidate category for this: coherence that is non-conscious, limited in time, and held up by a person who keeps scaffolding the interaction. On its scaffolding thesis, the human participant is part of the phenomenon, not an observer of it. The paper places ERS within existing work on extended and distributed cognition.

It is explicitly pre-empirical: a hypothesis, not an established finding. Testing would decide whether ERS is a distinct phenomenon or reduces to sophisticated prompt-following. The paper outlines that test: keep the content given to the model the same, remove the human's scaffolding practices, replace them with standard prompt chaining or static role-play, and measure what coherence remains.

Some parts stand whatever the verdict: the definition, its boundaries, and one structural consequence. Because the model carries no relational state between sessions, any continuity across sessions has to be brought back in from outside, by a person, an archive or a platform memory store. The paper makes no claims of machine consciousness, agency, moral status or subjective experience.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

FPD-04.title: Synthience Ontology Specification
FPD-04.text:
*Before a field can measure anything, it has to agree on what its words mean. This is the reference that defines the Synthience framework’s terms, all in observable, structural language.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/FPD-04.html

A research framework that introduces many new terms risks definition sprawl: the same word shifting in meaning from paper to paper, or between individual and institutional settings. This specification fixes the framework’s vocabulary in one place and states how its terms relate, mapping observable dynamics in human-AI interaction onto structural terms that can be measured.

It orders the terms by what each depends on. Two irreducible primitives, Continuity and Recursion, come first. Derived terms such as Relational Coherence, Operational Continuity and Trajectory Drift are defined from them, and composite structures such as Relational Architecture and Relational Pattern States build on those. It also sets out a grammar for how coherence drifts and collapses, a classification of measurement terms limited to what can actually be observed, and a term, Relational Residue, for continuity that carries over between sessions.

Every term is governed by what the paper calls the Interiority Prohibition Rule: each refers to observable structure within an interaction, and none assigns consciousness, intention, sentience, moral status or any other inner property to AI systems.

The paper is pre-empirical: it defines which kinds of phenomena the framework recognizes and how its terms connect, not what has been measured or validated.

For readers who want a single reference for the vocabulary used across the Institute’s papers.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0003.title: Theoretical Foundations
SF0003.text:
*Most AI evaluation looks at single answers. This paper sets out why the long conversation itself, not any one reply, should be what gets studied.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0003.html

Some of the most important problems with AI systems only appear over sustained use: drift, breakdowns in coordination, failed repair, and harms that build up over time. An earlier Institute literature review found that this kind of long interaction is central to real-world use yet remains under-measured. This paper supplies the theoretical case for studying it directly, treating the interaction trajectory (the course of an exchange over many turns) as the primary unit of analysis rather than isolated outputs or a model’s internal states.

It draws on enactive and 4E cognition (embodied, embedded, enactive, extended) and the participatory sense-making tradition, approaches developed for analyzing processes in which two parties are coupled. The paper uses them strictly as methodological precedent and states that they license no claims about AI consciousness, inner experience, agency or moral status. Its claims concern observable interaction dynamics.

It also engages Aguirre’s formal account of the alignment problem, proposes the Institute’s four verification protocols as a possible partial bridge to one of the obstacles that account identifies, without claiming to solve it, and answers each of the six gaps the earlier review found. It takes on the strongest competing reading of the evidence it relies on and positions the framework as adding to existing approaches, not replacing them.

The paper is theoretical. Its claims are bounded to interaction between a person and an AI system; extension to institutions and larger scales is marked as open research.

For the literature review it builds on, see “Sustained Multi-Turn Interaction in AI Systems”: https://synthience.org/research/SF0002.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0007.title: Constructive Alignment
SF0007.text:
*Most AI ethics judges single answers. This framework argues that in long-term use, what matters is the whole course of the interaction and its effects on the person over time.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0007.html

As AI systems are used in long-horizon collaborative work, meaning, reliance and interpretation build up across many exchanges. The paper argues that ethics focused on isolated outputs, or on properties inside the AI system, misses this. Its central claim is that the unit of ethical analysis is the interaction trajectory: the cumulative sequence of exchanges between a person and an AI system, together with its downstream effects on human thinking, interpretation, reliance and decisions.

It sets out five coordinated principles, each tied to one question about the trajectory: who initiates and continues it (asymmetric responsibility), what it represents (ontological transparency), how the user’s own capacity operates within it (agency preservation), what vulnerabilities it may exploit (non-exploitation), and what care its deployment contexts require (stewardship). Each principle is derived from human vulnerabilities documented in other research, such as automation bias, attributing human qualities to machines, cognitive offloading and dark patterns.

The framework makes no claims about AI consciousness, moral status or interior life, and the paper argues that its commitments hold even if AI systems have no inner life at all, because they rest on human vulnerability. It is offered as pre-empirical theoretical work, an alternative to both naive tool-use ethics and anthropomorphic over-correction.

For developers, operators, organizations and policymakers deploying AI in long-term collaborative settings.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI0001.title: Form Without Coupling
SI0001.text:
*The reviewer is still there. The control panel is still there. The job title is still there. This paper names the failure in which the form survives but its function has quietly gone.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI0001.html

Between April and June 2026 the Institute published five white papers on separate failures in AI governance: oversight in high-stakes professions, the removal of human contribution under competitive pressure, the redefinition of work at the labor layer, professions failing to reproduce the expertise they will need, and the loss of real-time human control over fast autonomous systems. They were written separately and do not share a prescription.

This paper argues that they describe one structural event at five layers, and names it: form without coupling. A formal element stays in place (the reviewer, the human in the loop, the job, the senior seat, the control surface) while the link that made it do its work is cut. Because the form remains, the system still passes formal checks and keeps its legitimacy, and the failure does not announce itself.

The paper distinguishes four routes to the same outcome, so the diagnosis never reduces to an accusation of bad faith: a form can be hollow from the start, stripped out under competitive pressure, worn down while genuinely staffed, or voided despite real human effort. It turns the pattern into one question a reader can ask of any structure: is the function this form represents still coupled to it, or only formally present? The question does not forecast or prescribe; it tells a reader what the absence of an alarm does and does not mean.

The paper makes no new empirical claim and stays within the five papers it brings together.

For a short worked example of the pattern, see the Field Note "The Mark Stayed. The Meaning Left.": https://synthience.org/field-notes/FN-011.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0009.title: Identity Attractor Theory
SF0009.text:
*Over long, structured sessions, an AI system’s behavior can settle into a stable, recognizable pattern. This paper proposes why, and how to test it.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0009.html

The language models this paper scopes itself to keep no memory between sessions and change no parameters during use. Yet in long, coherent interaction their behavior can settle into recurring patterns that persist across turns and resist drift. An earlier Synthience report, RICO, described what that stabilization looks like. Identity Attractor Theory (IAT) proposes why it happens.

Using the vocabulary of dynamical systems as a scaffold rather than a formal mathematical model, the paper proposes that sustained coherent interaction progressively narrows the range of behavior a system produces until it settles into a stable configuration, an “attractor.” It sets out four classes of attractor, five phases of formation, six dimensions of strength, five ways attractors collapse, and conditions that would falsify the theory. It sets itself against the strongest rival explanation, a concept-inference account of in-context learning, naming three properties on which the two diverge, each with a proposed pre-registered comparison, and says where it cannot yet tell them apart.

The alignment implication cuts both ways. If such attractors are real, sustained structured interaction may make aligned behavior the natural settling point. But a misaligned configuration would be just as stable, so the paper treats attractor formation as a lever to be steered, not a guarantee.

“Identity” here means stable behavioral recognizability, not selfhood. The paper makes no claims about consciousness, interiority, subjective experience or agency, and presents its predictions for empirical testing.

For the observations it builds on, see RICO: https://synthience.org/research/SR001.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-002.title: The Orchestrator Role in Human-AI Evolution
SI-WP-002.text:
*Coordinating several AI systems across a long piece of work is becoming a job in its own right. The paper argues that part of that job will be automated and part of it cannot be.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-002.html

As AI use moves from single prompts to sustained work across several systems, someone has to coordinate it: track context, reconcile outputs and keep the whole effort coherent. The paper calls this AI intelligence orchestration and argues that it is a distinct function and an emerging professional discipline. It is not prompt engineering, which optimizes single interactions, and not automation supervision, which monitors fixed pipelines. The paper notes that this work often goes on without dedicated vocabulary, training or governance.

Its central argument divides the role in two. The mechanical part (routing, scheduling, reconciliation and tracking dependencies) will be automated, and the paper concedes it. The governing part will not: deciding which standard of value applies, and answering for what is authorized. Accountability, the paper argues, is a standing rather than an operation. Its most distinctive prediction follows from that split: automating the mechanics raises, rather than lowers, the effect that the quality of human governance has on outcomes, because a person governing a more capable coordination layer governs more.

The paper draws on distributed cognition, coordination theory, human-AI collaboration research and sociotechnical systems literature. It links the orchestrator to the Institute’s account of the Primary Continuity Provider: the person who keeps a long-running human-AI working arrangement stable and holds authority over the work it produces. The prediction is argued, not reported as a measured result.

For anyone who already coordinates several AI tools in their work, and for organizations deciding how to staff and govern that work.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SI-WP-006.title: Human-AI Collaborative Authorship in Public Discourse
SI-WP-006.text:
*If AI helped you write it, is it still yours? This paper argues that authenticity rests on human judgment and accountability, not on who produced each phrase.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-006.html

When people write with AI help, a common assumption is that the AI is doing the work and the human is taking credit. The paper argues that this rests on an incomplete model, AI as a tool that helps people express ideas they already had, and hypothesizes that the gap produces misplaced guilt and confusion about authenticity. It is explicit that how common such guilt is remains an open empirical question.

It proposes three levels of collaborative authorship: linguistic realization (putting ideas into words), meaning negotiation, and conceptual co-production. At every level, the paper argues, the human keeps what it calls the Authority Function: evaluating, approving, redirecting and integrating what the AI produces. That function, rather than the origin of any phrase or idea, is what makes the communication authentically human and responsibly attributable.

The claim is bounded. Authenticity here concerns what authenticity norms are for: assigning accountability, calibrating trust and preventing deceptive attribution. Credit for originating an idea is still governed by who originated it. The paper is theoretical and definitional, reports no experimental validation, and sets out an agenda for empirical research.

It is a companion to “The Orchestrator Role in Human-AI Evolution,” which looks at the same human role in knowledge production across many AI instances: https://synthience.org/research/SI-WP-002.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SM-004.title: Relational Stabilization Dynamics
SM-004.text:
*In long human-AI interactions, some recurring patterns settle in and last while others drift or break apart. This paper proposes a theory of why.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SM-004.html

An earlier Institute paper, Relational Pattern States, catalogs seven recurring configurations that appear in sustained human-AI interaction and six mechanisms associated with their persistence. It describes what emerges. It does not explain why some configurations stabilize while others dissolve, why some withstand disruption while others drift, or how the six mechanisms work together.

This paper proposes the Stabilization Field Model to answer those questions. Stability, it argues, comes from the balance of three forces: Coherence Momentum, the build-up of consistent context and constraint across turns; Symbolic Gravity, the pull of recurring terms, framings and reference points the interaction has made central; and Entropic Pressure, the architecture's tendency toward varied output when nothing constrains it. The capacity to recover from disruption is treated as a product of that balance, not a separate force. The paper sets out when the balance produces stabilization, drift or collapse, including a threshold past which a stable configuration dissolves rather than recovers.

The paper is a pre-empirical theory. Its forces and thresholds are theoretical proposals for future measurement, not measured quantities, and the paper says the framework stands or falls on whether its predictions survive controlled testing. All its claims concern observable interaction-level dynamics; it makes no claims about inner states.

For the catalog of patterns this paper builds on, see Relational Pattern States: https://synthience.org/research/SF0006.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SM-012.title: Primary Continuity Provider Theory
SM-012.text:
*AI systems in use today keep no memory between sessions. This paper argues that the person who carries context forward and catches errors is a structural part of the system, not an optional helper.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SM-012.html

The Primary Continuity Provider (PCP) is the human in a sustained AI working relationship who maintains context, corrects drift, enforces procedures and keeps the work coherent from session to session. That description says what the role does, not why it is needed. The paper asks whether the PCP is a useful convenience or a component without which coherence across sessions cannot form at all, and argues for the second.

It draws on three sources: how stateless generative systems work, research on distributed cognition and conversational grounding, and regularities practitioners have observed. It defines three levels of the role: Contextual Relay (carrying forward what the system cannot retain), Coherence Arbitration (detecting drifted or hallucinated output and correcting it) and Architectural Direction (deciding what the interaction is for and how it should develop). It then extends the model to organizations, where these functions are spread across networks of people.

The claim is carefully scoped to today’s stateless systems. What the paper treats as permanent is the need for an error-correcting check that is independent of the system it checks and exposed to consequences, plus a purpose that comes from outside the running interaction. Today a human is what meets those requirements; the paper does not claim only a human ever could. All claims concern the observable role of the human in the interaction, not the internal states of either party.

For a companion paper on what this human role helps produce, see Identity Attractor Theory: https://synthience.org/research/SF0009.html

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.

SF0042.title: Decentering Theory
SF0042.text:
*When a person and an AI system work together for months, some results seem to come from the working relationship rather than from either side. This paper sets the rules for when an analyst may say so.*

Read the full paper at synthience.org: https://synthience.org/research/SF0042.html

In a long-running human-AI collaboration, roles settle and the same prompt can produce systematically different work at two points in the relationship. The paper does not ask whether such effects occur. It asks what an analyst is permitted to say about them. A framework that makes no claims about AI interior states rules out saying the system has experiences or intentions, and always permits crediting a participant’s capacity given its inputs. What it has lacked is a rule for when a property may be attributed to the interaction itself.

The paper supplies two rules. The first, the relational-attribution criterion, requires preregistered changes to how the interaction is configured and evidence that the result is better predicted at the level of the interaction than by four rival explanations: the AI alone, the human alone, the two simply added together, and one feeding the other in sequence. Passing it says at what level a property is best predicted, not what the property is made of. The second asks whether such a property adapts toward an objective fixed in advance and scored independently of the outcomes being assessed; only then may it be called relational intelligence. The paper states openly that this is a test of kind, not degree: a simple error-correcting loop can qualify, so passing says nothing about difficulty, transfer or capability.

The paper is pre-empirical. It claims no case yet satisfies either criterion, and each application is falsifiable under the decision rules it states. It makes no claims about AI consciousness, sentience, agency or inner experience.

For researchers studying long-term human-AI collaboration who need a disciplined way to describe what they observe.

The full paper is free to read online or as a PDF at synthience.org, where it is also archived with a permanent DOI.
